lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Restoring our basement, we were done. Like others who flooded that day, we were told it had been a 1-in-100-year rain event, a line that I myself repeated to many people last fall as a way to understand why the city's drainage could not keep up and why so many people had flooded. A few days after our basement was finally finished, the unthinkable happened. At approximately 1:00 a.m. in the early morning hours of September 12th, Water began pouring up out of our basement drain with so much force that we didn't even have time to elevate anything or take anything out. Our entire basement was flooded for the second time in a year, this time within minutes, and the water didn't stop coming in for over 4 hours. It is difficult to put into words how devastating and demoralizing flooding is one time, let alone 2 times or even more. The emotional, physical, and financial toll is significant, and my family is not the only ones. Dozens and dozens of homeowners, renters, and businesses are in the same situation as us. Consider the couple in their 70s who told me they had to borrow money to pay for their rental last year and are still making payments. Their basement filled with 3 feet of water this time, and they will have to borrow further to fix it again. Not to mention, they said, who's going to want to buy their home now that it has flooded twice? Their retirement is being upended. Consider all those living in basement suites who lost everything they had and don't have the luxury of living upstairs while their basement is being restored. Consider all those who can no longer get flood insurance and have to cover expenses entirely out of pocket. Consider all the people who are now living in fear every time they see a rain cloud. Consider those whose biggest asset, their house, is losing resale value. Thank you. We can say that these 2 rain events were outliers, but the fact is many people on my street have flooded multiple times over the years, and there are other areas of the city that have experienced regular flooding as well, whether overland or from drains. Where is the urgency to deal with this from the city side? I have heard the theories about how the city's drainage is supposed to work, but that is not the reality of what is happening. We say infrastructure is a city priority, yet we have areas that continue to flood. We essentially use streets and private parking lots as retention ponds so water can't drain fast enough in big rains, and this causes overland flooding. We say people shouldn't drain their sump pumps into the city system, but they are adding to flooding from drains. These big rainfalls are not supposed to happen this frequently, yet they have happened twice in one year. We have to start looking at what is happening, not what should happen. Thank you. There is a drainage issue and we need to do something about it. Not in the 5-year plan, not in the 10-year plan, but now. This has to be a priority, even if it means we have to move other projects around, or if it means we need to fast-track our climate change adaptation plan in order to secure funding from the federal government to deal with this. We need to figure out what is going on and increase our capacity to drain, reroute, or divert water faster. And if temporary measures need to be implemented while a long-term solution is figured out, we need to do that too. To the residents who flooded last week, my heart goes out to you, and I commit to keeping this at the forefront until something is done about it. Thank you.

And yes, we will work on our climate mitigation— climate change and adaptation plan, and we will find out what we need to know. Thank you. And we'll get those projects done. We need to get the projects done that will have the biggest impact, that will take care of the emergencies that we need to take care of today. And council will be committed on that as well. To all of you that have come tonight that have experienced flooding, we feel for you. We hurt for you. When a few people in our neighborhood Hurt, our whole community hurts, and we hurt for you as well. And we we will, as we said, we will commit to making sure that we will do everything. lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. So my question is to the city manager. I note that you're recommending approval if council has no concerns. It'll be obvious when I quote this why I'm asking. Part of what his report says is that the footprint of the duplex being proposed takes a higher percentage of the lot's total area than a typical residential lot. This increases the impervious area of the lot and will increase the stormwater runoff. When the development was designed, each lot was assumed to have the average impervious area to determine runoff. This assumes the houses on the lots will comply with the city setback requirements. In general, one lot with an increased building footprint would have a negligible effect to the stormwater management system. However, by allowing one lot, it sets a precedent for additional requests, and each increase in runoff reduces the storage and space available in the system, which would necessitate expanding the subdivision development's stormwater management features. In previous requests for reduced setbacks, which council's approved, one of the setbacks was not met. Thank you. However, there was more than the required distance for the other setbacks. This helped reduce the overall building area on the lot and the amount of stormwater runoff. So obviously, in light of, you know, recent events and just how flat our city is, we are sensitive, and we should be, to the issue of stormwater. So my question to the city manager is, could you just sort of outline why that— why the recommendation is to approve rather than to deny?

lines.text: I have a question for administration.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor

lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I have some concerns over this because of our own minor hockey and our minor sports programs that have lost ice while we were— this— our event centre was under construction. This is for a 5-year agreement. Did they request at all why it was a 5-year agreement, not

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager

lines.text: That was not a question that administration asked of SEG.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor

lines.text: So I appreciate the fact that the question was asked, the impact it would have on minor sports programming and rentals, and they did answer that question, that now we have 2 full services in operation and that it has not— the flex has not impacted minor sports. What if minor hockey sports What if they add a girls minor hockey program in 3 years from now and they're out of ice? We're going to get the pressure here to add another ice sheet. Is there, is there any of that dealt with in the memorandum of understanding?

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Nothing is specifically worded that way within the memorandum of understanding. However, with the overarching operating agreement that the City of Steinbach has entered into with With SEG Inc. Part of that operating agreement obligates SEG Inc. to follow the city's principles and policies within its ice allocation policy, which speaks to how ice is allocated to the various user groups in Steinbach, including minor sports and local user groups.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor

lines.title: Councillor

I would like to make a motion that this is, instead of a 5-year agreement, that this become a 1-year trial agreement Instead of a 5-year agreement that we— that it— the motion is to make it a 1-year agreement, not a 5-year agreement. Okay.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)

lines.title: City Manager

lines.text: Just to clarify, the recommendation from administration is that city council ratify the proposed operating agreement between the Eastman Selects and the Southeast Event Centre as proposed, subject to the execution of the proposed MOU between all parties.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor

lines.text: Essentially, yes, because the terms in the operating agreement that the City of Steinbach has entered into with SEG Inc., it obligates that any user agreement that is entered into by SEG with a user that is given occupancy of duration Yes. It doesn't speak to the city necessarily managing how agreements get determined other than the fact that the city needs to be a signatory to any agreements that do get prepared. The city, of course, has to, you know, be a signatory to any external agreements, and that's what this is. And again, our package, there are a number of things that are specifically, that are specifically addressed. And so I'm not prepared to substitute my judgment on the, you know, the quality of the agreement for the city manager's. What we don't know about the Southeast Event Centre Is we haven't operated for a full year. So what effects will other events have on it? The Grand Slam of Curling is coming in January. That's going to— the ice won't be available in the event centre for 10 days. That's going to affect minor hockey. It's going to affect all hockey, but minor hockey will be affected the most. They'll likely be the first ones bumped. But— and so how do you plan around it? So that's the first year of operation for the Southeast Event Centre. It is a— we don't know what the effects this is going to have. So this is a regional team. It's not a community team. This is a regional team. This is a feeder into the Pistons. I guess it is seen as that as well. So it's appropriate that, I guess, that they play here, but they feed into our minor hockey. Prior to the event centre even being announced, being built, minor hockey was before us. Minor sports, not just minor hockey. Thank you. That included ringette and figure skating and girls hockey, that they needed additional ice here in Steinbach. They were already then talking about a 3rd ice sheet. We just replaced one ice sheet. We didn't add any more ice. So this could potentially put us at risk again that we, that we will have a delegation before us for more ice again because there isn't enough because of this. On the other hand, We need— our minor sports needs to— it'll be incumbent on them to use ice that is available to them. There is a comment in here from the Southeast Event Centre that says that local minor sports won't be impacted. That's today. 3 years from now, if minor hockey— because we've got a lot of excitement with the Pistons in town, we've got a lot of people want to try hockey— if they want to grow their programs and they want to add 2 or 3 more teams, In minor sports, they can't because all that ice has now been allotted and committed for 5 years to the Southeast, to the Eastman Flex potentially. Those are the fallout of the law of unintended consequences that we're making here. So I don't either know what it's going to look like. I don't know what— but just on principle alone, and I don't want to micromanage here either. I appreciate that comment because that is not what we want to do.

Okay, Mr. Warkentin, we're— we have your, your information was given to us.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk

lines.text: In the rainstorm.

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Yep. The, uh, this, uh, report I have prepared for council, uh, again was submitted to, uh, to Council in their mail bins earlier this afternoon. The the rainstorm that the city experienced last week was significant. Administration has gathered information related to the storm event, and we're pleased to provide this summary report of the observed impacts. Approximately 126 millimeters of rain was recorded over a four-hour period at the city's weather station located at the. Steinbach Fire Hall at 477 Main Street, with reports of up to 135 millimeters of rain during the storm, or the equivalent of 2 months' worth of rain for Steinbach, as reported by CBC News in its online news article published on September 12th. We've also learned of localized areas in Steinbach reporting significantly higher amounts. This storm resulted in the accumulation of significant amounts of water and the inundation of wastewater and drainage systems that far exceed levels seen during normal storm events. In a story published by Steinbach Online on September 24th, 2024, David Phillips, a senior climatologist with Environment Canada, indicated that that storm saw 95.9 mm of rainfall over Steinbach on September 17th, 2024, and, uh, his quotes, ranks with some of the highest single-day totals over the last 6 decades, end quote. He further indicated that the previous wettest day in Steinbach since 1956 was the storm of July 4th, 2002, where the provincially reported official daily rainfall totaled 132.8 millimeters. Based on the rainfall reported in last week's storm and the city's observed impacts, this event appears to be of at least a similar intensity. General observations of city staff during the event found that because of the amount of rain that fell in such a short period of time, city's drains and ditches were operating at capacity or saw water spilling over their banks. All city storm drainage systems and wastewater system infrastructure was operating at capacity until well after the storm ended. In several locations, city roads had water accumulations exceeding 2 feet in depth, particularly at major drain crossings. Steinbach Lift Station 1 is located on Park Road West and pumps all Yes. Lift Station 1 is responsible for diverting all wastewater collected from the city's sanitary wastewater system to the city's wastewater lagoon. This lift station has automated pumps and remote monitoring systems to assist in its operation. However, city staff also complete regular daily in-person monitoring, operation, and maintenance at the site. City staff were called out and on site at Lift Station 1 on September 12th, 2025, beginning at 12:00 PM. Thank 12 you. midnight to manage the station operations both during and after the storm event. The Lift Station 1 stormwater pump activated at 12:12 AM with the maximum pumping capacity reached by 1 AM. The stormwater pump was shut down at 7:54 PM, approximately 20 hours later, with the operating levels at the station returning to normal by 8:20 PM. The maximum system flow rate was recorded at the station at 3:20 a.m. and reached 465 litres per second. The rated maximum capacity of the stormwater pump is 434 litres per second. Lift Station 1 equipment and systems were fully functional before, during, and after the storm of September 11th and 12th. All other city lift stations were fully operational before, during and after the storm. The city has been notified by several dozen Steinbach property owners to advise of water infiltration in basements both during and after the storm. Detailed information as to the circumstances of the private property flooding is not known with certainty. However, possible causes that could be the result of several factors such as overland flows through windows, infiltration from basement floor drains, failure of wastewater backup prevention devices, inadequate sump pump capacity, infiltration through basement plumbing fixtures, or any combination of the above. The T.G. Smith Arena was affected by overland flooding, as has been reported, and as a result, the ice surface was lost. Ice restoration is in progress, and the rink is anticipated to have its ice surface re-established and reopened to users by September 24th. Based on the city's landfill site entry records, demolition debris consistent with storm-damaged material from dozens of properties across the city has— have been deposited since Friday, September 12th. The most intense periods of the storm occurred overnight from September 11th to September 12th. The city's operations employees and many departments were available for duty and were called in outside of normal working hours and allocated as necessary to respond to a variety of storm impact mitigation efforts both during and after the event. Now, despite the city's observations that drainage and water— wastewater systems were fully functional and operating at capacity, the unusual and unexpected volume of stormwater significantly exceeded the design limits of Go ahead. This storm caused significant damage to the city's infrastructure and facilities. According to the city's understanding, the rainfall intensity and volume exceeded a 1-in-100-year storm event, which is far beyond the reasonable planning level for underground pipes and typical major drainage controls. During storms of this magnitude, overland flow, which is water moving along streets and low areas, can occur even when infrastructure is operating at full capacity. And in many locations, the The storm's intensity is likely to have contributed to the impacts on private properties. From 2021 to 2023, the city conducted modeling of its wastewater system to assess its capacity to address both short-term growth needs and to plan for long-term development opportunities in the city. The city's construction program to improve wastewater infrastructure has been in place for decades, and it incorporated the modeling information into to the annual wastewater infrastructure capital improvement programming. This has resulted in the completed projects to improve the Loewen Boulevard lift station, Loewen Boulevard sewer mains, and the PTH 12 North sewer main, and includes the recommended 2026 improvements to the Millwork Drive sewer main, the Park Road West sewer force main, and the Park Road West lift station. City Council also approved funding for the completion of a climate adaptation and mitigation planning project in the city's 2025 budget. This plan will highlight recommended steps the city can implement to improve the climate resiliency of its infrastructure and services. This project has started, is currently underway, and is expected to be completed in the spring of 2026. The city has also been in contact with Manitoba Emergency Measures Organization since the event regarding the provincial disaster Disaster Financial Assistance Program and has publicized information about the EMO Storm Damage Cost Recovery Program that may be available for affected property owners. And this information is available on the city's website and social media channels. Administration will continue to assess the available information resulting from this event and, along with information about other community needs, present this information to city council to consider its relevance in any future planning of the city's infrastructure network, project budget approvals, policy development, or for the planning of future development. Thank you.

This is the— this is our bylaw 2244, the official community plan. This is our 3rd reading. We had 2nd reading. It went off to the minister. Minister's approved. Now it's coming back for a 3rd reading. Is there any— anything you'd like to add, Mr. Warkentin?

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: I'm sorry, on what?

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: On the official community plan.

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Of course. How could I forget? I apologize. Given the recent few days, I seem to have zoned out slightly, so. The city's primary planning document is its official community plan. It provides a key overarching framework that provides the basis for the city's zoning bylaw, And numerous other planning and development policies affecting the city and developers and residents and property owners. This official community plan is something that under the Planning Act is legislated to be reviewed by municipal governments every— at least every 5 years. The previous official community plan was approved in 2018. Thank you. And the city administration initiated the review of this document in 2023 with the full intentions to meet that 5-year deadline. Unfortunately, as projects go, this one has stretched a little bit longer than what was expected. However, I am pleased to report that the official community plan, as was presented to city council on April 1st, 2024, 2025 at the city's required public hearing was submitted to the Minister of Municipal Relations as is required under the Planning Act, and I am pleased to report that the minister has indicated his approval of the city's proposed official community plan as is provided in the information package that is part of council's agenda. And accordingly, with minister approval, city council may now proceed to give this bylaw 2244 third reading, which would then make this bylaw effective and also rescind the existing official community plan bylaw 2099.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Warden. So, council, would you like to proceed? Susan Penner.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Motion to approve.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Seconded by Councillor Zwaagstra. Go ahead.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. As, uh, Mr. Warkentin said, this is an important planning document, the planning document for our community, and I, uh, feel like we, we did give this one a lot of thought. Every 5 years comes around quite quickly, so you Yes. You do it once and then maybe 5 years from now you kind of, huh, it's pretty close to what, you know, was the previous 5 years. But this one I feel like we did, you know, make some changes and to reflect what's happening, to reflect what's happening in the city. Sometimes you anticipate and project what's going to happen and it's not how things evolve. So I think this better reflects what's actually happening in our community. I see that maybe if I could I do believe we had some objections, and I'm assuming the minister said no, it's good to go.

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Correct. There, there were objections, some of them which were filed by adjacent municipalities to the City of Steinbach. Those, as are required under the Act, did get submitted to the minister along with the city's proposed OCP. I am pleased to report that the minister approved the city's OPP without amendment.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: That's excellent, and I just wanted to get that on record because I think that that is important. Anyways, I'm pleased to move the motion for this document.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Anything further?

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Obviously, official community plan is something that we do every 5 years, and I agree with Councillor Susan Penner that 5 years does seem to come around quickly. I'm pleased that the minister has approved this without any further amendments. And it's also true that I think we went through a very extensive process of consultations, and we had that very interesting public hearing on April 1st, 2025, which I will forever remember. So where we certainly looked at many different aspects of this. And so I think that the fact that the minister's approved it is a good signal that

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor) [medium]
lines.text: Anything further?

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything in closing?

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Nothing further.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Yes, council, we did— we spent a lot of time on this one. This one we worked on a little longer than we normally would have, and then it got tied up in the minister's office for a while. But I really think this is a good plan. The changes we've made in here are going to help us go in and get a lot of the things that we've been Into the future. And I'd just like to call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. We've come to council question period. Is there any questions of council? Okay, seeing none, we've got correspondence, petitions. We've got 11A. This is the Eastman Municipal Community South Subcommittee minutes of April 18th, 2018. Council meetings are held on March 18th, May 5th, June 9th, and August 27th of 2025. Councillor Siemens, I know you want to make some comments on this. You guys meet an awful lot.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Once a month, Mr. Mayor. At least that's how it started. Thank you, Mr. Mayor. A couple of comments. The ERMC, I think, is an important placeholder in our In what we— how we act as a council, just want to— we've been in existence for approximately 1 year, and we do meet once a month. It will be more frequently as minister meetings are coming up in September and October. But the ERM— ERM— ERM— Council. Or Eastern Regional Municipal Council, or committee, consists of 12 municipalities. We've all signed an MOU Stating that we will be part of it. That MOU is important to the province of Manitoba. That indicates that there's interest as we forward our concerns. And we, we talk and deal with regional concerns. The Premier has appointed Brandon Burley to our— to be the provincial rep on the committee. And we are the southern portion of a— Region. The northern portion also has a committee similar to this, but we are the only area in the province that has this. And this is similar to the major centres that you sit on and often invite council to. Issues that are being discussed: highway upgrades, specifically Highway 12, 52, and 59. And we talk about various intersections, so we want to have that impact into the highways minister. Lack of cell service, again highlighted during spring fires. Not everything that we talk about affects Steinbach directly, but indirectly it absolutely does. Water mitigation is one of them. Now, a lot of the water coming in Steinbach comes through Steinbach, and we're dealing with those as well. We speak to those issues as well. Downloads for the local fire departments, lift support, highway traffic accidents, how we get funding for that and how we don't get funding funding for that and download by the province on that. Water retention and mitigation, I talked about that, how water flows through Steinbach from local RMs. Well water from the Sandylands Provincial Forest, this is an aquifer that Steinbach draws all its water from. That today is potentially being threatened again by water co-ops in central Manitoba as they are looking again and starting to make requests to draw down that water for their own uses instead of just taking it out of the Red River. So that is also part of our discussions. Bridge replacements that aren't happening, that affects our customers coming into Steinbach. Healthcare in all communities with the LPN training and ensuring Steinbach has adequate staff for new addition. When we met with the Health Minister on September 4th, that was one of the things that we talked about when we met with her. Support major centres issues like doctor training in Brandon and bail reforms. So we also, as an organization, we write letters and copy letters to the ministers responsible both provincially and federally to support what Major Centre is doing. And it does have an impact because they— we hear back from ministers at different AMM events, and they have started to recognize what we do. On September 4th, we met with the Health Minister at Ste. Anne Hospital on a tour and had discussions. We're meeting September 22nd with the regional highways representatives here to speak about our local highways issues. And on October 22nd, we're in Winnipeg meeting with Minister of Highways, Minister Naylor, on various highways issues in southeastern Manitoba. And like the major centers, it works together on larger issues. And while the ERMC is just a similar— but we We work at the regional issues, whereas this major centre works at provincial issues. And the MOU again was signed by 12 municipalities. It's an important piece, as Minister's Office can address all 12 municipalities in the room at one time and in one location. We seem to be getting traction, and it feels like we're being heard. I think it is an important piece, place for our council to be a part of.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you, Councillor Siemens. And you did mention, you know, Cities Caucus Several times, and I feel that together as a province, our advocacy is gaining traction. I think I think with the NDP, you know they're listening. They're they're opening the doors. We've had in Steinbach. I would say Steinbach alone has had multiple minister meetings. Actually, Councillor Susan and I were at a. At a meeting this afternoon, and we said that. We can't believe how many ministers are coming to Steinbach and listening and wanting to hear us and going back and actually advocating for us. And I think it's great, and I think the more we advocate together, the more our voices say the same thing, the better our position in the province gets. Call for the question. All those in favor? There's no question. Oh, no, no, sorry.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: There's no motion.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Man, we've been talking about this so long, I thought we had to make a motion. Okay. Sorry. So we'll take this information. Great. And the Steinbach Arts Council, this is referring to the grant increase. This is a letter of— I believe a letter of thank you from David Clausen for the increase in our funding to their program. You know, council, this doesn't always happen very often that, you know, we get a nice thank you like this from an organization that we work with in our community, but this is very good. I know they're very thankful. I was at their AGM last week and very solid community organization and their net revenue has exceeded $1 million a year. Like, they are really growing and they're growing fast and they're becoming a very solid financial organization. So council, take this information. No other business. Looking for a motion to adjourn. Councillor Penner. Second. Second by Councillor Hiebert. The question, all those in favor? Opposed? That's carried. Next regular council meeting is Tuesday, October 26th.
